module_title: Memory Units - Word Length, Machine Dependencies, and Theoretical Units
introduction: Tailored for SSC CGL Tier-2 (Mains) and technical IT Officer exams, this advanced module explores the concept of 'Word Length' inside CPU architecture, differentiates between 32-bit and 64-bit systems, and reviews the exact fixed capacities of legacy storage media.

core_concepts.title: Word Length (Word Size)
core_concepts.description: Beyond Bits and Bytes, a 'Word' is the natural unit of data used by a particular processor design. Word length defines the number of bits a CPU can process simultaneously in a single operation. Unlike a Byte (which is always fixed at 8 bits), Word size is strictly machine-dependent.

core_concepts.title: 32-bit vs. 64-bit Architecture
core_concepts.description: If a CPU has a 32-bit architecture, its Word length is 32 bits (4 Bytes). A 64-bit CPU processes 64 bits (8 Bytes) in a single cycle. This makes 64-bit processors fundamentally faster and allows them to address significantly more RAM (beyond the strict 4GB limit of 32-bit systems).

core_concepts.title: Theoretical Units Beyond Yottabyte
core_concepts.description:
While YB is the largest official SI-recognized binary prefix, theoretical computer science concepts extend further:
- 1 Brontobyte = 1024 Yottabytes
- 1 Geopbyte = 1024 Brontobytes (Currently considered the highest theoretical unit of memory).

core_concepts.title: Standard Legacy Storage Capacities
core_concepts.description:
Advanced exams frequently test the exact maximum capacities of older physical media:
- Standard 3.5-inch Floppy Disk = 1.44 MB
- Standard CD-ROM = 700 MB
- Standard Single-Layer DVD = 4.7 GB

important_entities.name: CPU Registers
important_entities.significance: The size of a computer's 'Word' is directly dictated by the physical size of the internal Registers built into the CPU core.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A common statement-based trap claims '1 Word is universally equal to 2 Bytes'. This is false. While a Byte is universally fixed at 8 bits, a 'Word' scales with the processor (it could be 16-bit, 32-bit, or 64-bit).

Strictly speaking, the math for a 1.44 MB floppy disk is a bizarre hybrid of decimal and binary measurement (it actually holds 1,474,560 bytes, not 1.44 * 1024 * 1024). For exam purposes, simply memorize the final standard label: '1.44 MB'.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: To remember the theoretical units that follow the Yottabyte, remember 'Big Giant': B (Brontobyte) -> G (Geopbyte).

exam_strategy_tips: In Tier-2 analytical math questions, you may be asked: 'In a 64-bit processor, how many Bytes make up one Word?' Simply divide the bit architecture by 8. (64 / 8 = 8 Bytes).
